newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Russian worries may tarnish Bunds.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Russian worries may tarnish Bunds.

text.p: German Bunds and the mark may lose some of their shine amid concerns about the state of Russian President Boris Yeltin's health, analysts said on Thursday.

Benefitting from a traditional "flight to quality", the dollar will remain firm as news about Yeltsin's latest illness filters through, providing an impetus for switching out of core European markets into T-bonds.
But the impact will be only slight -- at least for now. "Yeltsin's illness provides another reason to buy Treasuries," said Adrian Owens at Julius Baer Investments.
"With the 10-year yield spread to Bunds at 74 basis points, the U.S. market is looking quite attractive."
Yeltsin, who only returned to the Kremlin on December 23 after recovering from heart surgery in November, was taken into hospital again on Wednesday suffering from pneumonia.
Although his condition is being described as "quite satifsfactory", natural concerns about the 65-year-old's health are already seeping into foreign exchange markets.

"The key question is the impact on the German mark, which has traditionally always been highly exposed to eastern Europe," said Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"But I'm a sceptic when it comes to the influence of Russia on the markets now."

German assets used to be hyper-sensitive to Russian risk, both because of bank loans and trade flows. But the end of the Cold War, coupled with progressive economic liberation in Russia, changed the situation dramatically.
"Russian/Western relationships have been become enormously multilateral," said Baader. "But there will still always be a small impact on the deutschmark."
"Clearly, when things start to go badly in Russia, the dollar recommends itself because people begin to worry about whether a bi-polar world will emerge again," he said.

For now, analysts said the market impact of Yeltsin's illness would be marginal, but they said a more significant shift could come about if he were to die, leaving the volatile country leaderless and unstable.

In that scenario, analysts predicted a sharp knee-jerk reaction, with the dollar likely to jolt higher against the mark, pulling Treasuries into outperformance and tightening the T-bond/Bund 10-year yield gap.
Beyond the initial days, it would be a question of watching and waiting.

Political commentators say stability may well be maintained, with Anatoly Chubais, the chief of the Kremlin administration, and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin stepping in to hold the fort as they did when Yeltsin was out of action in November.

But risks may crop up, with the likes of Alexander Lebed on the sidelines. Lebed, who was sacked by the Kremlin in October after he warned of potential mutiny within the Russian army, said earlier that Yeltsin's latest illness had left a political vaccuum and he should resign
"The assumption will be that Chernomyrdin will take over in the near term. But if things start to get really messy further down the road, markets will see more of an impact," said Owens.
The main fear would be the risk to the process of economic reform presented by any change in leadership, said Nick Stamenkovic, European economist at DKB International in London.
If progress were hampered, investment in Russia would begin to dry up, translating into negative market sentiment towards Bunds and the mark, he said.
But Stamenkovic noted a "cry wolf" atmosphere in global markets, saying that significant market gyrations were unlikely to arise from the Russian political situation.
"Traditionally when you have problems in Russia it has a damaging impact on the Bund market," he said. "But each time we have had problems, the impact has been less and less."
"This could have an immedite negative effect on Germany, but I don't think it will be sustained."
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
